Use all FF* codes for: Stories about crimes, or mysteries to be solved, locked room mysteries, whodunits, heists and capers novels, crime novels, detective stories, murder mysteries, cold cases, unsolved crimes, etc. Use all FF* codes with: other codes for different types of crime fiction that do not have a unique code, for example, with PLACE 1* qualifiers for regional crime fiction, FK* for horror crime fiction, FL* for science fiction crime
Also class here: Classic whodunit stories. Use for: works of crime fiction widely regarded or presented as ‘classic’ and typically, but not necessarily, published and in print for several decades

Also class here: Amateur sleuths, religious sleuths, private investigators, silver-haired sleuths, accidental detectives. Use for: stories where the main investigator is not an official police or judicial investigator
Use for: contemporary mysteries set in past times, e.g. in Victorian, Medieval, Roman period. Use with: PLACE 1* and/or TIME PERIOD 3 * Qualifiers to indicate setting as appropriate

Also class here: Cozy crime, cozies, Cottagecore crime, domestic mysteries, soft-boiled crime stories, pet mysteries, cats or dogs mysteries, cooking mysteries, academic cozies, craft or hobby mysteries, cozy silver-haired mysteries. Use for: mysteries set in rural or traditional communities featuring minimal violence and typically amateur sleuths
Also class here: Funny or comedic crime and mystery stories

Code.CodeDescription: Misdaad en mystery: hard-boiled crime, fiction noir
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: Roman noir, domestic noir crime stories. Use for: crime or detective stories often featuring things like gritty urban settings, bleak landscapes, or places that have been broken or distorted by crime, morally compromised or complex protagonists, dark mysteries, or a bleak, pessimistic or dark outlook on human nature, pessimistic vision of a place. Use with: PLACE 1* qualifiers to indicate setting, for example, Nordic noir crime stories set in parts of Scandinavia, Mediterranean Noir, American Hardboiled, etc Zie ook: FHR

Also class here: police and forensic investigation, judicial or detective investigators, undercover police operations, police stories, forensic pathologists, coroners, forensic anthropologists, crime scene investigators, covert policing, undercover cops, plainclothes detectives, etc

Use for: Crime or mysteries where the mystery is solved by a woman, and where the woman is the detective, investigator, police officer, or other person who investigates or solves the crime or mystery etc. Use with: other FF* codes to indicate the genre as appropriate
Use with: S* codes to indicate specific sport featured

Use all FH* codes for: conspiracy thrillers, disaster thrillers, Eco-thrillers, classic thrillers, assassination thrillers, vigilante justice thrillers, kidnapping or murder thrillers, domestic thrillers. Use all FH* codes with: other F* codes as appropriate for different types of thriller or suspense fiction that do not have a unique code, such as FL* for Sci-fi thrillers, FRM for Romantic thrillers, FK for Horror thrillers, FJM* for military thrillers, FV for historical thrillers, JBGX for thrillers about conspiracies, FXS for Social thrillers, FF* for crime thrillers

Also class here: Spy novels, stories featuring cold war spies, secret agents, undercover agents, spy agencies or intelligence agencies, counter-intelligence, state intelligence services, intelligence officers, secret services, secret police, spying or intelligence gathering, assassins or assassination plots in the world of espionage, etc

Also class here: thrillers featuring white-collar crimes, crimes of corruption, fraud or greed. Use for: thrillers in which the financial system, the world of finance and money, the financial markets, the economy, big business, world of corporations, multinational or transnational business or corporations, financial professionals, business people, corporate bosses, wealthy business families or dynasties, or similar play a major role

Also class here: Cyber thrillers. Use for: thrillers incorporating scientific, technological (including computing digital technologies, artificial intelligence), etc. elements as important parts of the narrative

Use for: thrillers that usually feature something used for medical purposes becoming a weapon or threat, such as a virus, often featuring medical practitioners as key characters, biological threats, pandemics, medical forensic practitioners, etc

Also class here: Courtroom drama thrillers, thrillers featuring lawyers, judges, prosecutors or other legal settings or roles, or politicians, the world of politics or political settings, including political plots, political assassinations, political conspiracies, political targeted killings, etc

Also class here: Occult, supernatural, mystical thrillers, archaeological thrillers. Use for: thrillers featuring traditions of ancient, secret or esoteric knowledge, such as the Holy Grail, or thrillers with occult, supernatural or mystical themes, conspiracies around secret or occult organisations or structures, etc.

Use for: thrillers based around criminal organizations, the criminal underworld, the mob, the mafia, crime syndicates, criminal gangs, contract killers, hired killers, professional gunmen, assassins, hitmen or hitwomen, criminal gangs, criminal feuds, criminal families, gangland crimes, gangsters, gritty urban crime, etc Zie ook: FFL

Use for: thrillers based around mass murderers, serial killers, spree killings, thrill killers, angel of mercy or angel of death type killers, etc. Use with: FK* for horror stories that include serial killers
Use for: thrillers based around potential terrorist actions, acts of terrorism, terrorist plots, political terrorism, conspiracies to commit acts of terror, anti-terror plots, etc

Also class here: Domestic thrillers. Use for: thrillers that deal with a psychological narrative, or are told from the viewpoint of psychologically stressed characters, or where the plot concentrates on investigations of the psychologies of the principal characters, thrillers that examine things like perception, reality, the mind, identity, existence or purpose, etc Zie ook: FXM

Use all FJ* codes for: adventure stories, stories of exploration, classic adventure or action stories. Use for: works that primarily emphasise physical, and sometimes violent, action, that often have a sense of danger and are meant to give the reader a sense of excitement or adventure Zie ook: FH
Also class here: wuxia, Bukyō. Use with: FM*, FV*, XQ* codes plus TIME PERIOD 3* Qualifiers as appropriate
Use for: adventure novels set in past times. Use with: PLACE 1* and/or TIME PERIOD 3* Qualifiers to indicate setting as appropriate. Prefer: specific FJM* code if applicable Zie ook: FJM

Code.CodeDescription: Fictie over oorlog, gevecht en legeravonturen
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: Special forces stories, historical military fiction. Use for: stories that primarily emphasise the action or adventure side of war or combat. Use with: PLACE 1* and/or TIME PERIOD 3* Qualifiers to indicate setting for historical war or combat fiction. Prefer: other F* codes and TIME PERIOD 3* qualifiers for works where war or conflict is part of the background of the story or that examine the impact of war but where the primary theme could not be seen as action or adventure

Also class here: stories set during the French Revolutionary Wars, the Coalition Wars, the Peninsular Wars, the War of 1812 or any other associated war or military campaign of this period. Use with: PLACE 1* and/or TIME PERIOD 3* Qualifiers to indicate setting as appropriate
Also class here: naval and maritime fiction, nautical fiction. Use for: adventure or action stories featuring seafarers, pirates, sailors, fishermen and so on, or largely set at sea

Use all FK* codes for: monster literature, Lovecraftian horror, cosmic horror, Eldritch horror, psychological horror, folk horror, body horror, transformative gore, survival horror, haunted house horror, extreme horror, demonic horror or any stories that provoke or inspire feelings of dread, fear and terror, or are intended to disturb, frighten or scare, using psychological or supernatural elements, or any story that includes a ghost, or the possibility of ghosts, or a characters belief in ghosts. Use all FK* codes with: VXQ* codes if appropriate, for example with VXQG for ghost stories, VXQM2 for vampire, werewolf or shifter horror, VXQM3 for zombie horror, VXQM5 for demon horror, VXWT for stories featuring evil witches and other F* codes, for example, FU* Comedy horror, FL* for Horror Science fiction, FP for Erotic horror, FV for Historical Horror, FLQ or FDB for Post-Apocalyptic Horror, FF* or FH* for Crime horror or thrillers with a horror plot, FHX or FXM for Quiet or psychological horror, FYL for Gothic horror, or with 5* Qualifiers, for example, 5HPD for Christmas Horror, 5HRD for Winter Horror, etc Zie ook: FMT FHX

Also class here: classic gothic horror. Use for: supernatural fiction, horror or ghost stories widely regarded or presented as ‘classic’ and typically, but not necessarily, published and in print for several decades
Use for: supernatural fiction, horror or ghost stories set in the present day or contemporary settings, typically first published in the last few decades

Use for: works where major themes of the story deal with the darker side of witchcraft, spiritualism, psychic phenomena, demonic possession, satanism, mysterious or secret knowledge, or other paranormal phenomenon

Use all FL* codes with: other subjects codes or qualifiers for different types of SF that do not have a unique code, for example, FU for Comical (humorous) science fiction, Sci-fi comedy, 5PS for LGBTQIA+ science fiction, 6JM for Indigenous Futurisms in SF, with 6AR for Afrofuturism (African-American / Black American / African diaspora SF), or with 6AS Africanfuturism (African) in SF, FK* for Science fiction with horror stories Zie ook: FD FDM
Use for: science fiction widely regarded or presented as ‘classic’ and typically, but not necessarily, published and in print for several decades

Also class here: Chuanyue, Isekai, stories based on travelling to a past or future time via time loops, time machines, time slips, time portals, accidental time travel, alternate timestreams, time warp, temporal paradoxes, experiencing time in reverse, communication from the future, being stuck in a time-loop, stories where time is a significant element, different spacetime geometries, wormholes in spacetime, stories based on the quantum mechanics of time travel, temporal war, etc. Use with: FM* codes for time travel or time slip fantasy stories, with FDK for alternate history science fiction, featuring alternate futures, different timestreams, multiple time paths

Use for: science fiction that emphasises scientific detail and / or accuracy, or that use science that exist within the realm of scientific possibility or do not go outside the known physical laws of the universe

Use for: science fiction stories that have a more positive, lighter and more comforting, feel-good or uplifting approach to telling the story, and that tend not to create any anxiety, often featuring narratives around hope and optimism, friends or friendship, found or chosen family, communities, and where conflicts or crisis are usually resolved through communication and understanding, with the help of community and friends, often stories with elements of science fiction, but where world-building is not a major element

Also class here: dieselpunk, retrofuturism, stonepunk, atompunk, decopunk, clockpunk, steelpunk, rococopunk, silkpunk, arcanepunk. Use for: science fiction based on an alternative world where 19th century steam power has emerged as the dominant technology, or any other retrofuturistic ‘punk’ genre where a certain technology from the past has become dominant

Also class here: AI takeovers, robot uprisings, super robots, intelligent technology, genetic engineering, artificial intelligence, alternative realities. Use for: sci fi set in a very near future, from the creators point of view, and in a world that is a natural progression from their own, that often feature current technologies or technology in development and its effects upon the world, that may feature things such as advanced high tech, artificial intelligence, robots, Mecha, cyborgs, transhumanism, the technological singularity

Also class here: Nanopunk, Cyber-noir, solarpunk, techno-noir. Use for: science fiction based on marginalised or low-life characters in a highly technologically advanced society or focused on the implications of biotechnology or genetic engineering

Also class here: end of the world stories, dying earth, collapsing or collapsed civilization. Use for: stories set in worlds trying to prevent, or experiencing or that have already been affected by an apocalypse event, such as runaway climate change, an impact event, resource depletion, nuclear holocaust, pandemics, plagues, viruses, the end times, a zombie apocalypse, cybernetic revolts, technological singularity, invasion from space, dysgenics, an electromagnetic pulse (EMP), stories of groups of survivors or survival after a catastrophe or cataclysm etc. Use with: FXE for climate fiction or ecological collapse, FXV for stories of journeys through a devastated world or other codes and qualifiers as appropriate
Use for: science fiction set within the military or where organised use of weaponry is central to the plot Zie ook: FLS
Also class here: Galactic empires, planetary romance. Use for: science fiction set in space, usually with advanced cultures and technology
Also class here: first contact, alien invasion, human interaction with extra-terrestrial life forms, alien conspiracies
Also class here: colonisation of space, settlement of planets or moons, exploration of deep space, moon bases, generation ships, terraforming, first landings on other planets, astronauts

Use all FM* codes for: Classic fantasy, other worlds fantasy, Crossworlds fantasy, Futuristic fantasy, Portal fantasy, Parallel worlds, Quest fantasy, Literary fantasy, Hard fantasy. Use all FM* codes with: other codes for different types of fantasy that do not have a unique code, for example, with 5LKE for New Adult Fantasy, 5PX-XA-A for Arthurian fantasy, VXQM1 for dragon fantasy, 5PGM for Christian fantasy, 5PS, 5PT, 5PU or 5PV for LGBTQIA+ fantasy, FXB for coming of age fantasy, FU* for Comic fantasy, 5YH for Anthropomorphic fantasy, FDB or FLQ for dying earth or post-apocalyptic fantasy, FP for erotic fantasy or FRX for Erotic Fantasy Romance, FXP for Political fantasy, FLM for Steampunk fantasy, FJW for Weird west fantasy, FL* for Sword and planet fantasy, 6AU for Academy fantasy, etc
Use for: stories set in alternative or secondary worlds, usually with detailed world building and a complex fictional universe or shared world, and often involving large events or long quests

Also class here: Swashbuckling fantasy. Use for: works of fantasy that concentrate more on the adventures and battles of the hero or main protagonist, rather than the world building, or fantasy stories that feature a hero, anti-hero or morally grey hero going on some sort of quest or any sort of hero‘s journey in a fantasy or supernatural setting where the narrative concentrates more on the adventure rather than building the fantasy world. Use with: other FM* codes as appropriate

Also class here: Medieval, Dark Age, Classical (Greek and Roman), Arabian, Celtic, Fantasy of Manners, Mannerpunk, Flintlock, Gunpowder, Prehistoric, Gaslamp fantasy genres. Use for: fantasy that incorporates fantastic elements, such as magic or elements from myths, into recognisable historic settings, periods, cultures etc. Use with: PLACE 1* and/or TIME PERIOD 3* Qualifiers to indicate setting as appropriate

Use for: fantasy stories that have a more positive, lighter and more comforting, feel-good or uplifting approach to telling the story, and that tend not to create any anxiety, often featuring narratives around hope and optimism, friends or friendship, found or chosen family, communities, and where conflicts or crisis are usually resolved through communication and understanding, with the help of community and friends

Also class here: Magic realism. Use for: works that incorporates fantastic, magical, mythical or supernatural elements into an otherwise real-world or mundane setting, stories that have a largely realistic view of the world but with a few supernatural or magical elements, that are often used to make a point about reality. Use with: FBA or FBC for literary works that incorporate magical realism, for example, those of the kind frequently associated with literature from Latin America or other literary traditions

Also class here: Romantasy, fantasy with a romance element. Use for: fantasy stories using many of the elements and conventions of the romance genre but that remain primarily and recognisably a fantasy story, where the main plot is a fantasy story but with a strong romantic sub-plot. Use with: FRX for romantic fantasy stories with a more erotic or sexual storyline, or other FR* or FM* codes as appropriate Zie ook: FRV FRT
Use for: fiction featuring or where the main characters are depicted as superheroes / superheroines or superhumans

Also class here: Grimdark. Use for: fantasy stories with darker and frightening themes, often incorporating elements of horror or that have a gloomy and threatening atmosphere or a sense of horror and dread

Also class here: intrusion fantasy, mundane fantasy. Use for: fantasy set in the present day or contemporary or modern settings or set in a recognisable version of our world, but with elements of fantasy or the supernatural added in

Also class here: Elfpunk, Arcanepunk fantasy, gritty urban fantasy. Use for: fantasy works set in urban settings, often featuring plots where the real modern urban setting and the supernatural or paranormal collide or overlap, or where mythical or supernatural beings and creatures exist in recognisable urban settings. Use with: VXQ* codes as appropriate

Code.CodeDescription: Fictie: Traditionele verhalen, mythes en sprookjes
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: Fables. Use all FN* codes for: stories that often have a long and continuous existence through multiple generations, stories that get told and retold, traditional local folktales, tall tales, folklore, folk literature, wisdom tales, cautionary stories, teaching stories, origin tales, or any form of traditional story told or retold. Use for: modern retellings in novel form or collections of traditional tales and stories aimed primarily at adults, or works inspired by these stories Zie ook: DBS* QRS* JBGB YFJ YNRU

Code.CodeDescription: Sprookjes en volksverhalen / Hervertellingen van sprookjes
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: folk and fairy tales from any culture told in a story form, or fantasy retellings of these stories, fairy tales as fiction, fairy tale fantasy. Use for: modern retellings in novel form or collections of these types of traditional stories aimed primarily at adults, or stories recognisably inspired by traditional fairy stories or that in some way draw from the characters, tropes, themes and symbolism of folklore and fairy tales and where, for example, an author might tell a new story based on a popular fairy tale or character from a classic work, or take a ‘what if’ approach or create a mashup of different genres, for example, fairy tale meets dystopian future Zie ook: JBGB YFJ YNXB4

Also class here: Mythological Fiction, Legend fantasy, Mythic fantasy, myths and legends from any culture told in story form, myth or legend retold as fiction, or genres such as mythpunk, godpunk, Shenmo, Gods and Demons fiction, Xianxia, Immortal heroes fiction, Arthurian fiction, Classical (Greek and Roman myths told as stories or retold). Use for: modern retellings in novel form or collections of these types of traditional stories aimed primarily at adults, or stories recognisably inspired by traditional myths or stories that draw from the characters, gods and goddesses, heroes and heroines, tropes, themes and symbolism of myths or legends and where, for example, an author might tell a new story based on a myth, or take a ‘what if’ approach or create a mashup of different genres, for example, mythology crossed with contemporary adventure story. Use with: QRS* or QRR* codes or PLACE1* qualifiers to indicate which tradition, as appropriate Zie ook: DBS* JBGB QRS* YFJ YNRU
Use for: stories that feature a trickster character such as a spirit, a deity, a human or an animal, or stories inspired by or retellings of stories about trickster characters from different cultures

Also class here: Erotic literature. Use for: stories aimed at adults of an erotic nature that deal explicitly with sexual relationships and themes, that are not primarily a romance story. Use with: other F* codes for genre fiction that is also erotic and with 5PRD for erotic novels about BDSM, fetish or kink sex or other erotic subcultures and INTEREST Qualifier 5X as appropriate. DO NOT USE: with FRX code Zie ook: FRX

Also class here: feel-good fiction, cozy / cosy fiction, up-lit, ‘slice of life’ fiction. Use for: stories set primarily in the present day or contemporary settings, dealing with realistic everyday themes or lifestyles, usually in a light-hearted, sometimes uplifting, manner, often focusing on things like the everyday trials and tribulations of the main protagonist, their friendships, their found families, relationships, ups and downs of life, their workplace or professional life, or their place of education, their day-to-day lifestyles, their social life, their emotions, or may be life affirming stories about everyday characters which champion empathy, understanding, kindness, stories of everyday joy or sadness, everyday hope and optimism, etc. Use with: other F* codes for particular genres Zie ook: FRB FRD

Use all FR* codes for: Love stories, classic romance, slow burn romances. Use all FR* codes with: qualifiers for particular types of romance, for example, with 5H* qualifiers for Holiday Romance, such as 5HRB for summer vacation romance or 5HPD for Christmas romance, 5PS* or other 5P* qualifiers for LGBTQIA+ romances, 5LKS for romance in later life, FL* codes for Science fiction romance, FJ* for action and adventure romance, JBSE for small town romance, 5PB-US-C for Black and African American romance, 5HKU for Romance about marriage, FYL for Gothic romance, 5LKE for New Adult romance, etc
Also class here: Rom-coms. Use for: genre romance and love stories that are also comic, humorous, light hearted or funny in their approach

Use for: romance stories where the main characters live and work in a world most readers can understand, with modern conveniences and current social mores. Use with: other FR* codes and qualifiers for particular sub-genres of contemporary romance, and with qualifiers as appropriate

Use for: romance and love stories that have a more positive, lighter and more comforting, feel-good or uplifting approach to telling the story, and that tend not to create any anxiety, often featuring narratives around hope and optimism, friends or friendship, found or chosen family, communities, and where conflicts or crisis are usually resolved through communication and understanding, with the help of community and friends

Also class here: First job romances, office romances, forbidden workplace romance, love in the workplace, professional romance, renovation romance, working from home romance, boss romance. Use for: Romance stories featuring or set in a working environment, or about a relationship with a work colleague or a romance with a person who is doing some work or working for the other person, for example, someone who is helping to renovate a building, doing some long-term construction work, the gardener, the boss, the CEO, the bodyguard, etc

Also class here: sweetheart romance. Use for: romance that does not contain any strong language or physical intimacy. Use with: FW for religious romance, faith-driven romance, or inspirational romance, and with 5PG* INTEREST Qualifiers as appropriate to indicate a wholesome romance with themes inspired by a particular spiritual belief or faith or with other FR* codes for wholesome romances that are also considered part of another genre romance, with 5PB-US-B for Amish romance, 5PGM for Christian romance, 5PGP for Muslim romance, etc

Also class here: Student romance. Use for: genres of romance fiction often set in an academic environment such as a university or a college campus or an academy, usually featuring university aged characters discovering life as newly adult people, getting their first taste of adult love, romance and often sexual experience. Use with: 5LKE if the main characters and the storyline concern the newly adult or those young adults who have left home for the first time

Use for: romance stories set in the past (typically before the writer’s lifetime), where the time period is a significant or essential part of the story, and that portray the spirit, manners, and social conditions of that time with realistic detail (e.g. Regency romances, Victorian romances, US Civil War, Gilded Age, Belle Epoch romance, Arthurian romance, Medieval or Renaissance romance, Tudor romance, Romances set in the Ancient world or romances featuring Vikings, pirates, Scottish highlanders, knights, etc). Use with: PLACE 1* and/or TIME PERIOD 3* Qualifiers to indicate setting as appropriate,

Also class here: cowboy, cowgirl, frontier, rancher, rodeo, gaucho, vaquero romances. Use for: romance that takes place in very rural environments, often set on farms, ranches, haciendas, or in small rural communities, usually far from any city and often set in the Western parts of the USA, Mexico or Canada, the pampas of South America, the Australian outback or similar environments. Use with: PLACE 1* Qualifiers to describe setting and TIME PERIOD 3* for historical settings

Also class here: Romance stories featuring extramarital love affairs, cheating love triangles, love triangle jealousy, or other stories featuring some sort of love triangle. Use for: romance stories usually featuring a triangle of relationships and typically involving two people who are competing for the third person’s romantic attention or one person in love with two different people

Also class here: second chance romance, neighbours to lovers, roommates to lovers, opposite attracts, unlikely loves, forbidden love, unforeseen romance, Grump and sunshine romances, sworn off love, etc. Use for: Romance where the plot revolves around a significant change or an adaptation of the nature of an existing relationship between the main characters
Use for: romance stories where the main characters initially have a relationship based on friendship that gradually changes into a strong attraction
Also class here: Rivals to lovers’ romance, Frenemies. Use for: romance stories where the main characters initially have a conflicting relationship that gradually changes into a strong attraction

Also class here: fake-dating, false relationships, fake boyfriend or girlfriend, marriage of convenience romances. Use for: romance stories where the main characters initially have some sort of fake or pretend romantic relationship

Also class here: Stuck together romances, Only-one-bed romances, road trip romances, trapped together romances. Use for: romance stories where the main characters initially are thrown together into close proximity for various reason
Use for: a romance story that also involves a mystery, crime, suspense or thriller storyline but remains primarily a romance story. Use with: other F* genre fiction codes as appropriate

Also class here: Athlete Romance, Football romance, hockey romance, baseball romance, cricket romance, soccer romance, etc. Use for: Romance featuring participants in sports, sports stars, athletes, coaches, owners, agents, sports teams, sporting events, sporting activities or any romance where the sports element is an integral part of the story. Use with: S* codes to indicate which sport is the key aspect of the romance story

Also class here: military, armed services, armed forces, security, sailors, aircrew, law enforcement, soldiers, sheriffs, cops, firefighters, police, pilots, cabin crew etc. Use for: romance stories where one or more of the main protagonists is in a job that means wearing a formal uniform
Use for: romance stories featuring doctors, nurses, surgeons, veterinarians, or any professional medical setting, such as a hospital or clinic, etc

Code.CodeDescription: Romantiek: de rijken, beroemdheden en machtigen
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: Rockstar romance, Rags to riches romance, Millionaire or Billionaire romance, Secret Billionaire romance, Celebrity romance, Royal romance. Use for: genres of romance fiction featuring persons in position of great wealth, power, status or similar, such as the jet set, super-rich, billionaires, royalty, aristocrats, rock stars, celebrities, high society, celebrity meets a non-celebrity and they fall in love, romance story featuring an ordinary person and a very rich, powerful, famous person, or romance fiction featuring at least one of the main characters who is royal or aristocratic or other inherited positions and titles, or featuring a royal kingdom or aristocratic domain, royal meets a non-royal and they fall in love, romance story featuring an ordinary person and an aristocratic or royal personage, etc. Use with: 5PDM* or other 5* INTEREST Qualifiers as appropriate

Also class here: ‘why choose’ romances, harem or reverse harem romances, polyamory romance. Use for: Romance or love stories featuring things like, open relationships, polyamorous relationships, polyandry, polyfidelity, consensual non-monogamy or non-exclusive relationships, or stories featuring multiple lovers, partners or romantic interests. Use with: VFVG2 for romances about polyamory, and with INTEREST 5* Qualifiers as appropriate

Also class here: vampire romance, were / shifter romance, supernatural romance, monster romance, alien romance, fantasy romance, paranormal romance. Use for: a romance story which blends elements from the fantasy genre or features mythical creatures or supernatural elements but remain primarily and recognisably a romance story, where the main plot revolves around a romance, with a fantasy or paranormal setting or with fantasy elements included. Use with: FM* or VXQ* codes as appropriate, for example for romance stories featuring a romance with vampires, werewolves or shapeshifters use with VXQM2, featuring demons with VXQM5, for angels, VXPS, ghosts, VXQG, witches VXWT, aliens VXQB, etc Zie ook: FMR

Also class here: romance and love stories based on travelling to a past or future time via time loops, time machines, time slips, time portals, accidental time travel, alternate timestreams, time war, temporal paradoxes, experiencing time in reverse, communication from the future, being stuck in a time-loop, accidental time travel

Use for: genre romance stories where the themes are darker, usually featuring an anti-hero or non-heroic characters and/or distressing situations, often exploring themes such as the darker side of power dynamics in a relationship, questionable morals or ethics, they may feature trauma and violence, or they may deal with darker psychological themes of evil or horror in society. Use with: 5X if appropriate

Also class here: Rebel and outsider romance, Mafia romance, Mob romance, MC Romance, Motorcycle Club Romance, Rogues, Rebels, and Rakes romance, Bad boy romance, Bad girl romance, Alpha Male romance, Bully romance, Biker romance, MMA romance, Fighter romance, or romances featuring characters such as assassins, criminals, outlaws, bandits, or morally grey characters. Use for: romance genre stories where one of the main protagonist is often a very strong, possessive, confident, and dominant male or female character, or romances where the main character works for, or is involved with, crime or criminal organisations, or is seen as an anti-hero, a wrongdoer, an outsider, or to have a bad or dangerous character, or is morally ambiguous, but the “bad” character will usually have a redeeming side or a change during the story. Use with: FJ* for action and adventure stories, with FHR or FFL for romance stories featuring organised crime, and with INTEREST 5* Qualifiers as appropriate. Prefer: FRV for romance stories with darker themes Zie ook: FRV

Also class here: Spicy romance, Steamy romance. Use for: romance fiction which contains explicit sexual content, or where the plot of the love story revolves around the sex, but which remains primarily and recognisably a romance story. Use with: INTEREST Qualifier 5X as appropriate, and with 5PRD for erotic romance stories revolving around BDSM, fetish or kink sex and other qualifiers and FR* codes as appropriate. DO NOT USE: with FP code Zie ook: FP

Also class here: family dramas, inter-family stories, family rivalries, stories about siblings, brother-sister stories, stories about twins, parent and child stories, etc. Use for: novels of domestic or small-scale family life, often with a focus on the relationships within a family – of any type – but not of the FT* Generational sagas genre. Use with: other F* codes as appropriate Zie ook: FT

Also class here: Multigenerational family sagas. Use for: genre novels which chronicle the lives and fortunes of a family or a number of related or interconnected families over a period of time and often over generations. These are often part of a sequence of novels. Use with: FR* codes for Romantic sagas or with FV when the historical setting is particularly important, for example for epic historical family sagas and PLACE 1* and/or TIME PERIOD 3* Qualifiers to indicate setting as appropriate. DO NOT USE: for traditional Icelandic or Old Norse sagas Zie ook: FS

Also class here: Comedic stories, comedy fiction, funny and comic novels. Use for: fiction where humour is the primary aim and feature except prefer genre-specific ‘humorous’ headings where available. Use with: other F* codes as appropriate, for humorous genre fiction
Use for: humorous fiction which is satirical and/or which parodies existing fiction, genres or writers Zie ook: WHP FYH

Use for: stories set in the past (typically before the writer’s lifetime), where the time period is a significant or essential part of the story and that portray the spirit, manners, and social conditions of that time with realistic detail. Use with: other F* codes as appropriate and PLACE 1* and/or TIME PERIOD 3* Qualifiers to indicate setting as appropriate. Prefer: genre-specific ‘historical’ headings where available Zie ook: FFH FJH FMH FRH

Also class here: faith-inspired or inspirational fiction. Use for: fiction designed to promote a particular religious, spiritual or visionary message. Use with: 5PG* values from INTEREST 5* Qualifiers as appropriate, or where unavailable, a QR* or VX* code and with other F* codes, for example FR* for Religious romance novels, with VX* codes for visionary or spiritual fiction, with 5PGM for Christian Fiction, etc

Use all FX* codes for: identifying the primary theme of a narrative work, when that theme is not conveyed by the choice of a genre fiction or manga, comic book or graphic novel category. Use all FX* codes with: FB* codes or other F* codes indicating genre or type, or with Literature DB*, DC*, DD* or Comics (Graphic novel / Comic book / Manga etc): genre XQ* codes, to indicate the principal underlying narrative theme of a work of fiction, literature, poetry, drama theatre, comic books etc. FX* codes can also be used in conjunction with non-fiction categories to give greater definition to the narrative theme where appropriate, FX itself can be used with a non-fiction code if there is not a suitable other FX* code. DO NOT USE: FX* codes as the primary or main subject code or simply to indicate a mood or emotion evoked by a story
Also class here: bildungsroman, growing up, rites of passage, passage from childhood or youth to adulthood as narrative themes, stories about a young person going from being a child to being an adult

Code.CodeDescription: Narrative theme: books and the world of books
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: stories, novels and works of fiction where the main theme is about the world of books, including, booksellers, bookshops, libraries, literature, writers, the art of writing, books about reading, books about books, book clubs, publishers or any story that has a main theme taken from the world of books

Use for: fiction where a strong relationship or love is the central theme but which is not a genre romance novel. This can include friendships, found family, family relationships, sibling relationships, parent-child relationships, any form of affective relationship, relationships between couples, relationships that are negative or hostile, or complex emotional relationships, forbidden love, a love triangle, unrequited love, love of family, relationships amongst a group of friends or a peer group, examination of relationships with others, acquaintances, strangers etc, as long as it is one of the principal themes of the story. Use with: INTEREST 5* Qualifiers for detail of specific kinds of relationships as appropriate. DO NOT USE: with FR* codes

Use for: fiction that addresses a specific environmental issue or nature-orientated topics as a central theme. Use with: other subject codes to give more specific definition to the topic if appropriate, for example, FD*, FL* , FF* or FH* codes for Climate fiction (Cli-fi), Eco-fiction or eco-thrillers or FB* for nature writing in fiction, or with XQ* codes for comic books, graphic novels or manga that have major themes around the natural world or the environment

Use for: fiction or stories that feature animals or any living creature as a major or significant part of the plot or theme, or where human interactions or relationships with animals, including pets, is a main part of the plot, or one or more of the main characters or protagonists are animals. Use with: WN* codes if the story is about a specific type of animal, for example, WNGC for stories about cats, or WNGD for stories about dogs

Use for: works of fiction that take place during periods of war or armed conflict or civil strife, and where the experience or consequences of war, or battle or armed conflict is the major theme or topic of the story and is explored through the plot or the development of the main characters. Prefer: FJM* codes for action and adventure war fiction Zie ook: FJM*

Use for: fiction where health, coping or living with illness – physical or mental – or the consequences of sickness is a central theme, or themes based on medical topics or suffering linked to physical or mental health, chronic illness or conditions, chronic pain, or themes around the healing, recovery or recuperation from illness

Use for: fiction where death, dying, the end-of-life, a loss or the experience of grief or mourning is a central theme and one of the key elements of the story, but not for genre fiction like crime, thriller or adventure novels that happen to have a death in them

Also class here: psychological realism, character-driven psychological stories, stories with an interior monologue or stream of consciousness. Use for: fiction which places particular emphasis on interior characterization, and on the motives, emotions, feelings and thoughts or mental lives of characters, stories that explore the mental state of a character. Prefer: FHX for psychological thrillers Zie ook: FHX

Use for: fiction where the identity, the sense of, or search for, identity of whatever kind – social, cultural, religious, gender etc, as an individual or part of a group – of the main character(s) is the main, or one of the main themes of the story, or narratives where the characters sense of belonging or search or need for belonging is the main or major theme of the plot. Use with: other subject codes and INTEREST 5* Qualifiers as appropriate

Also class here: Political novels, fiction as political or economic criticism, novels of political satire, fiction as commentary or discussion on politics, economics, society, government, diplomacy, politicians or political culture, political power, political corruption as major themes of a story. Use for: fiction or literature where political or economic concerns are the underlying narrative theme including political or economic allegories. Use with: DC* for political poetry. Prefer: FHP for political thrillers Zie ook: FHP

Code.CodeDescription: Verhalend thema: verdrijving, uitwijzing, verbanning, migratie
Code.CodeNotes: Use for: fiction that has major themes relating to diasporas, dispersion, asylum, deracination, forced relocation, cultural transitions, forced journeys, living in exile, being exiled, emigration, expatriation, immigration, refugees, forced resettlement, etc Zie ook: FXV

Use for: fiction set in a real location where the setting or landscape very deeply pervades the work to the extent that it could not be set anywhere else; e.g. the French tradition of ‘roman du terroir’. Use with: PLACE 1* Qualifiers, and other subject codes for example, with JBSD for novels where city life is a main theme, or JBSG for reservation life or rez lit, or JBSE for small town life novels, JBSC for works of fiction where the setting in a small town, village, a rural area, or in the countryside and the associated lifestyle or living conditions are critical to the sense and meaning of the story

Also class here: Social protest novels, fiction as social commentary, stories about social unrest. Use for: fiction that addresses a specific social problem or issue as a central theme, such as, poverty or precarity, economic inequalities, homelessness, housing issues, conditions in factories and mines, the plight of child labour, violence against women, rising criminality, and epidemics because of over-crowding and poor sanitation in cities or works of fiction in which a prevailing social problem, such as gender, race, or class prejudice, is dramatized through its effect on the characters of a novel. Use with: other non-fiction codes, especially JBF* codes, to give more detail of the main social issue but an F* code MUST be designated as the Main Subject

Use for: works of fiction where the main narrative theme or subject matter clearly illustrates topics relating to aspects of accessibility, social justice, equity or equality, diversity and inclusivity within the context of the story, or the story explores themes of DEI, or attempts to achieve DEI. Use with: other subject codes and INTEREST 5* Qualifiers to give greater detail as appropriate

Also class here: road trip stories, stories about voyages of exploration and discovery, stories about quests, epic journeys or about wanderers. Use for: fiction where a journey, expedition, voyage or some sort of travel or trip is the main or a major narrative theme of the story Zie ook: FXQ

Use all FY* codes with: other F* code indicating genre or subject, or with literature DB*, DC*, DD* or Comics (Graphic novel / Comic book / Manga etc), genre XQ* codes, to indicate the principal underlying distinct aspects, attributes, characteristic or features of a work of fiction. FY* codes should not usually be the primary or main subject code. DO NOT USE: FY itself - always use FY* codes
Also class here: Anthologies or collections of short works of fiction either by the same author or by multiple authors. Use with: DNT for anthologies of short stories by theme or by multiple authors
Use for: works of fiction that are neither seen as short stories nor as novels by their creators
Use for: fiction, literature, comic books or any fictional narratives that are written in a series of documents, letters, diaries, journals, emails, blogs, social media posts, etc

Also class here: Continuation novels. Use for: works of fiction where a new author continues an established series after the original authors death. These can be official with the permission of the literary estate or unofficial for works now out of copyright. These stories may be sequels to the original series or be stories that are prequels or precede the original storyline, but all the stories are written after the original authors death
Use for: fiction written deliberately in the style of another (typically earlier) author (as homage rather than parody) Zie ook: FUP

Also class here: Past-Present narratives. Use for: fiction, literature, comic books or any fictional narratives that have storylines featuring two or more timelines (but where there is no time travelling or time slips), where a single cohesive narrative, is told using multiple time periods and perspectives

Use for: fiction, literature, comic books or any fictional narratives that are usually create an atmosphere of tension and suspense for the reader using psychological techniques and often feature themes things like a sense of fear and haunting, gloom or death, a dark past, a claustrophobic atmosphere, an oppressive, bleak, decayed or derelict setting, the threat of supernatural events, and the intrusion of the past upon the present and that often inspire fear through a romanticized view of the past, and often combining elements of both horror and romance etc. Use with: FR* for Gothic romance, FK* for Gothic horror, other F* codes for other types of Gothic fiction, with PLACE1* Qualifiers for gothic fiction associated with a particular area, such as 1KBB-US-S* codes - for Southern Gothic (USA) or 1KL* codes for gothic fiction set in Latin America

Also class here: mash-up or mashed-up novels. Use for: fiction which combines a pre-existing text, often a classic novel, with another contrasting genre, such as horror, into a single narrative, or that takes fictional characters, settings, or universes from different fictions and places them into a single story. Use with: other F* or non-fiction codes to indicate component elements Zie ook: FUP

Use for: fiction based on or inspired by a true event or happening but where this is told in narrative fictionalised form and is not just an account of the event itself. Use with: other F* codes to describe the genre or with Literature DB*, DC*, DD*, comic books XQ* codes. Prefer: DNX for narrative accounts of true stories, or FC for fiction based on peoples lives Zie ook: DNX FC

Code.CodeDescription: Fictie: speciale kenmerken: Yaoi / BL romans
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: boys’ love novels. Use for: East Asian style stories, often related to comics or anime, featuring male same-sex relationships, created principally, but not exclusively, for a female readership. Use with: other F* codes to indicate genre, for example FR* codes for Romance stories, 5LKE * codes if they are about that generation Zie ook: XAMT

Use for: the kind of romance, science fiction or other types of genre fiction or comic books, usually published on a monthly basis, short, in clearly delineated lines and with a certain number published every month. Use with: other F* code indicating genre or type, for example, with FR*codes for Category or Series Romance. DO NOT USE: FYR as the main or primary subject or the only code

Also class here: Raito noberu, Japanese novellas, illustrated novellas. Use for: short fiction aimed at adults, usually driven primarily by dialogue and character and generally accompanied by illustrations in manga/anime or similar styles. Use with: other F* codes to indicate the genre. FYS may be used as a main subject as appropriate

Use for: fiction and literature translated from another language. Use with: F* or with Literature DB*, DC*, DD*, or comic book XQ* codes to ensure classification is meaningful beyond the translation of the work itself and with 5T* - Literature of Place Qualifiers as appropriate. DO NOT USE: PLACE 1* or LANGUAGE 2* Qualifiers to specify the original language (this is described in other metadata). You may still use a PLACE 1* Qualifier if it is relevant to the plot or setting of the book. DO NOT USE: FYT as the main or primary subject or the only code

Code.CodeDescription: Fictie: geïnspireerd door of aangepast van andere media
Code.CodeNotes: Use for: stories that were published as spin-offs or companions to pre-existing non-book media or merchandise, novelizations and novels inspired by a popular film franchise, an online game or a TV series. Use with: other F* codes indicating genre or type, or with Literature DB*, DC*, DD* codes if this work is presented as a poem or a play, or XQ* for comic book. DO NOT USE: for titles that were subsequently made into films, film tie-in versions (this is described in other metadata)

Also class here: GameLit, RoLit, Game lit, literary role-playing game. Use for: fiction that is structured like a videogame or role playing game, or features the same kind of challenges as would be found in any type of game, or is about or set in a videogame, an online game, a role playing game, etc. Use with: other F* codes especially FL* or FM* as appropriate, or with Literature DB*, DC*, DD* codes if this work is presented as a poem or play or XQ* for comic book

Use for: companion works to popular fiction or comic book series or titles, typically uncritical, such as an atlas or map of a mythical world or fictional universe, a compendium of characters or objects, to the flora, fauna or geography of the place, a guide to the series, art inspired by or taken from the series, a cookery book or crafts inspired by the series, etc. Use with: other F* codes indicating genre or type, or with Literature DB*, DC*, DD* or comic book XQ* codes if this work is presented as a poem or a comic book etc. Prefer: DS* codes for critiques or critical works Zie ook: DSR XR* DS*

Use all G* codes for: specialist and general adult titles. DO NOT USE: code ‘G’ itself, but select specific categories from section G*. Use all G* codes with: other subject categories and qualifiers where appropriate
Use for: non-subject-specific works only
Use with: other subject code indicating the area or scope of the work Zie ook: CB* DSR*
Also class here: Who’s Who. Use with: other subject code indicating the area or scope of the work
Use for: dictionaries and glossaries covering a particular subject e.g. Legal dictionaries. Use with: other subject codes as appropriate

Use for: reference works that present a subject primarily through maps, charts, infographics, data visualisation, visual timelines or other mainly visual presentation of information. Use with: other subject codes and qualifiers indicating the area or scope of the work. DO NOT USE: just to indicate a work is illustrated, use only when the work would not be understandable without the visuals Zie ook: RGX
Also class here: collections of common phrases or aphorisms, helpful quotations for specific purposes
Zie ook: AVD
Use for: works listing individuals or organisations (generally arranged alphabetically, thematically, phonetically, etc) with details such as names, addresses, and telephone numbers

Use for: works containing a mixture or assortment of pieces compiled from varied sources and that can include many subjects and be in a variety of different forms, such as quotes, facts, illustrations etc. Use with: other subject codes when the miscellany covers one broad subject, (e.g. for a bestiary use with WN* codes) Zie ook: WDKX

Code.CodeDescription: IT, internet en elektronische bronnen in bibliotheken

Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: indexing, cataloguing and classification
Also class here: academic, specialist, public and school libraries; reference, circulation and community services

Also class here: museum studies, curatorship, heritage interpretation, and historical conservation, collection management, museum administration, conservation of cultural heritage. Use for: works about the preservation and promotion of culturally and socially significant sites, buildings, monuments, the tangible, intangible and natural cultural heritage of a society, the historic environment, preserved cultural heritage, etc Zie ook: ABC AGC NK* RNK TNKX WTHM

Also class here: orality as a means of transmitting knowledge from generation to generation, use of oral storytelling for teaching and transmission of knowledge, Oral interpretation. Use for: works that look at the use of oral communication of stories, sacred narratives, texts, literature, kinship, music, laws, knowledge, learning, traditions, healing, natural world, agriculture or any other cultural element, or about the nature of oral story telling, orality and its important in different cultures, etc. Use with: other subject codes to indicate particular subject areas Zie ook: DH JBGB
Also class here: control and stability of systems, entropy

Also class here: data visualization and infographics, large data sets, big data, data governance, data analytics. Use for: interdisciplinary works about data, data management and its uses in other disciplines, works about techniques, methods, processes, algorithms, used to extract or extrapolate knowledge, information or insights from data, structured or unstructured). Use with: other subject codes as appropriate Zie ook: UN* UX* UYZF
Also class here: cryptography Zie ook: URY
Zie ook: KJMD
Also class here: risk management, risk analysis. Use with: other codes for works about risks in different sectors

Also class here: works on research methodology, research design, research proposals, research strategies, basic or fundamental research methods, Experimental research methods, research writings, writing for publication and presentation of research papers, comparative research methodology. Use with: other subject codes for research methods within a particular discipline. Prefer: subject codes alone for work about a subject even if it was based on or the result of research Zie ook: JHBC KJT
Also class here: Empirical research questions. Use with: other subject codes for empirical research methods or strategy within a particular discipline
Use with: other subject codes for quantitative research methods or strategy within a particular discipline
Use with: other subject codes for qualitative research methods or strategy within a particular discipline

Also class here: Applied research strategy, action research, evaluation research, research and development, practical applications of research, applying research to solve practical problems. Use with: other subject codes for applied research within a particular discipline

Also class here: Interdisciplinarity. Use all GT* codes with: other subject categories and qualifiers for works about different types of ‘Studies’, usually academic that include multiple subjects or disciplines, or works that are about cross-disciplinary research

Code.CodeDescription: Geschiedenis van de wetenschap (hoofdzakelijk sociale wetenschappen en geesteswetenschappen)
Code.CodeNotes: Use for: historical studies concentrating on fields of study not covered by the English term ‘science’ (cf. history of science), but included for example in the German term ‘Wissenschaft’ (i.e. all kinds of academic studies) Zie ook: PDA PDX

Also class here: Communication science. Use for: Communication Studies textbooks and for works covering a range of aspects of communication – linguistic, social, industrial, technological etc, works that look at ways of communication, or the means used to communicate, the means of transmission of information, Augmentative and Alternative Communication techniques Zie ook: JBCT*
Zie ook: CFA

Code.CodeDescription: Reception or Interpretation studies / Audience Theory
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: Hermeneutics, Interpretation of text, theories and methodologies of interpretation, or of audience reception. Use for: Interdisciplinary topics that examine how something has been perceived at different times, how things have been interpretated or how an audience has reacted to it. Use with: JBC* for audience theory in Media Studies, DBSS for Classical Reception Studies, QD* for Hermeneutics or Interpretation as a philosophical discipline or QR* for hermeneutics or interpretation in religion, especially with QRVC for the interpretation of sacred texts, NK* codes for interpretation in archaeology, ATFA for reception studies in film, DS* for reception studies and theories in literary criticism, etc
Use for: interdisciplinary works Zie ook: QDTM JM* MKJ PSAN UYQ* UXJ

Also class here: area studies, global studies. Use for: interdisciplinary works covering a range of topics within a defined geographical, cultural or linguistic area. Use with: PLACE 1*, LANGUAGE 2* Qualifiers as appropriate Zie ook: RGL
Zie ook: KCM

Also class here: epistemological or epistemic decolonization, decolonialism, works that explore the widening of an approach to knowledge or to what is studied and how it is studied. Use with: other subject codes for works that examine this in the context of a specific topic

Also class here: vexillology, symbology. Use for: general works about one or any of these topics. Use with: other subject categories as appropriate, for example, use with QR* codes for religious symbols, use with KJS* codes for logos or symbols used in marketing, VXW* codes for symbols associated with different mystical or magical traditions Zie ook: NHTG
Also class here: transitional justice, Reconciliation Studies, Peacebuilding, Peacekeeping, Peace and Reconciliation Studies, Transformative Justice as part of reconciliation Zie ook: JWLP
Zie ook: JPSN

Use for: usually interdisciplinary material aimed specifically at General Studies courses at undergraduate level or general knowledge and cultural information for adult education. Use with: with 4CN*, 4CP* or 4TN* for tests Zie ook: WDKX YPWL

Use all J* codes for: specialist and some general adult titles, but see also V* codes for practical approaches to many topics. Use all J* codes with: other subject categories and qualifiers where appropriate. In J* use the most appropriate code(s) available, as many social sciences are broad topics that can have many alternative terms or names

Use all JB* codes for: both general and academic works on social topics, general works about culture and society. Use with: JH* codes for sociology textbooks and other specialist works as appropriate Zie ook: VFV*
Also class here: general works on media and culture studies, works about the relationship between media and society, culture and cultural topics and their relationship to media

Also class here: intercultural studies, studies of cultural identity, general studies of cultural heritage, contemporary culture in society, cultural sociology. Use with: PLACE 1*, LANGUAGE 2* or 5P* INTEREST Qualifiers to indicate the cultural studies of a particular region(s) or country / countries, language grouping or groups of people
Also class here: Contemporary culture, pop culture, mass culture, culture of fame or celebrity, fan culture, fan studies, fandoms

Use for: the interdisciplinary field telling of relationships between people and their things, the role of artefacts and objects in society, the making, history, preservation, and interpretation of objects

Also class here: changing ideas of beauty or body image in culture and how individuals dress the body, works on aspects of attire, clothing, costumes, dress or fashions in different cultures or societies, or works that look at how dress is used within societies to communicate social status and social role, cross dressing in different cultures, etc. Use with: NHTB for an historical approach or AKT* codes as appropriate

Also class here: Food writing, cultural aspects of food and gastronomy, cultural aspects of cultivating, foraging, gathering, harvesting or hunting for food. Use for: works that examine the traditions, habits, customs, rituals, ceremonies, taboos linked to food and drink in different cultures, food or drink as intangible cultural heritage. Use with: NHTB for an historical approach and with WB* codes as appropriate Zie ook: WB

Also class here: studies of traditional rituals and ceremonies; cultural taboos or superstitions, social behaviour, values and norms as defined by society, institutions, traditions and cultural beliefs, studies of Intangible cultural heritage, traditional cultural expressions, traditional knowledge, cultural practices, etc Zie ook: JBGB

Also class here: Comparative studies, cross-cultural encounters, cross-cultural exchanges, cross-cultural clashes, intercultural relations, intercultural communication, interculturalism, cross-cultural conflicts, clashes of values or beliefs. Use for: works that examine social and cultural topics and issues around the meeting of or interactions between different cultures, including conflicts, negative or positive exchanges, on a personal or a societal level. Use with: NH* codes for historical topics

Use for: works about current debates, policies, ideas, controversies around the role of culture or cultural heritage in society, debates about clashes of cultural values or beliefs, debates about cultural imperialism, cultural diversity, the nature of culture, social and political policies linked to culture, debates about funding and political policies in culture
Use for: works that look at the expression, preservation, and change of human ideas over time. Use with: other J* or NH* or QD* codes as appropriate
Also class here: Media culture, Infotainment, Mass media. Use for: works that deal with the content, history, and effects of various type of mass communication media Zie ook: GTC

Code.CodeDescription: Mediastudies: Internet, digitale media en maatschappij
Code.CodeNotes: Use for: all aspects of online, digital and social media and their role or impact in society, including things such as blogging, tweeting, influencers, spread of real and false information, changing habits and behaviour linked to digital media Zie ook: ATN
Use for: works on both traditional and new forms of consuming small screen entertainment, including streaming and on demand services, impacts and influences on culture, links to popular culture, etc
Also class here: the Press, newspapers, news media, journalists and reporters, online and print journalism, communicating news and events Zie ook: KNTP

Also class here: propaganda, ‘fake news’, post-truth politics, ‘alternative facts’, doctored and fake photos, images, videos, deepfakes, use of artificial intelligence to falsify data or images. Use for: works about the purposeful use of false or misleading information, manipulation of thoughts and actions by use of information, the spread of misleading or non-fact based information, the selective use of facts, information or news stories, planting of stories in mass media. Use with: JBCT1 for works about the role of digital platforms or social media, with JBGX for misinformation or disinformation linked to conspiracy theories Zie ook: KJST JBGX
Use with: other categories to indicate works that treat a subject as part of a social, cultural or ethical debate and where there is no specific JBF* code Zie ook: PDR QDTQ RNT

Also class here: social exclusion, social inequalities, social marginalisation, diversity studies, hate speech, hate or bias crimes, intersectionality. Use for: works about various forms of discrimination, about equality or inequality, about prejudice based on a person’s identity, about systemic or institutional bias, and also about measures to address these issues, such as diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies or topics, equal treatment, positive discrimination, work on unconscious bias. Use with: other JB* categories, or other subject categories and Qualifiers to denote specific forms of discrimination, e.g. with JBSF* codes for sexism or discrimination based on sex or gender, QRAM9 plus 5PG* codes for discrimination based on religion or beliefs, JBSJ plus 5PS* codes for sexual prejudice or discrimination based on sexual orientation, JBFM and 5PM* Qualifiers for ableism or discrimination based on ability or disability, JBSA and 5PD* for discrimination based on class or socioeconomic status, with JBSP* and 5L* for discrimination based on age

Also class here: institutional racism, xenophobia, antisemitism. Use for: works about discrimination and prejudice based on skin colour, race or ethnic origin, or prejudices based on the perception that someone is foreign or from outside the community, and issues of inequality and discrimination, works that explore institutional or systemic racism, racial segregation, as well as measures to address racism, or to advance conversations about race, for works that look at other identities or perceptions of an identity, such as beliefs or religion, where the prejudice becomes or is treated as a form of racism. Use with: other J* codes for works about racism in particular domains and with 5P* INTEREST Qualifiers to indicate works about racism aimed at particular groups, for example, with 5PBD for works about racism aimed at those of African descent, with 5PGJ for works about racism aimed at Jewish people or on racial antisemitism, with 5PBA for works about racism against Indigenous groups, with 5PBR for racism against Romani or Travellers, etc
Also class here: full assimilation, assimilationism, acculturation, cultural integration. Use with: NH* codes for works that look at historical cultural or social integration

Also class here: forced religious conversion, forced cultural assimilation, forced cultural changes, or the use of educational, religious, official organisations or other institutions to eliminate cultures, languages, beliefs, individual or collective identities, or to force assimilation by a dominant, invader or colonial culture on a pre-existing cultural identity. Use with: NH* codes for history titles, such as NHTQ when linked to colonialism, NHTZ when linked to historical genocides, NHTT when linked to invasion, QRAM9 when linked to religious intolerance of other beliefs, JPFN when linked to Nationalism, etc

Also class here: the economically disadvantaged, extreme poverty, poverty threshold, works about food poverty or food insecurity, food banks, unemployment or employment when linked to poverty, the precariat, economic insecurity, underemployment, chaotic lifestyles, malnutrition linked to poverty, in-work poverty, the working poor, economic or income inequalities, economic disparity, wealth inequality
Also class here: the unhoused, issues around providing houses, cost of homes, lack of accommodation, etc

Use for: works about the consequences, on people and society, of natural, or human-made, emergencies, disasters and accidents; including things like: plagues, epidemics, pandemics, famines, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, extreme weather, severe storms, floods, droughts, fires, crashes, shipwrecks, maritime and air disasters or accidents, rail or road accidents, explosions, oil spills, getting trapped or lost, etc. Use with: VSY for titles that explain how to prepare for disasters, for example, what to do during an earthquake, or major fire or tsunami, etc Zie ook: RNR
Also class here: asylum seekers, sanctuary. Use with: other codes for specific topics, such as JBFA for discrimination, JBFD for housing topics, NHTB for social history, FX for novels, etc

Also class here: the Underground Railroad, the Comet Line, Fluchthilfe, etc. Use for: titles about helping refugees escape repression, slavery, conflicts etc. Use with: NH* codes and PLACE 1* and TIME PERIOD 3* Qualifiers as appropriate

Use for: works about diasporas, the expatriates, settlers or migrants themselves, or cultural or social topics linked to migration. Use with: other codes for specific topics, such as JBFA for discrimination, JBFD for housing topics, NHTB for social history, N* codes for the history of human migrations, movements and settlement, the Historical expansion, movement and migrations of groups of peoples across land and sea, historical movements of populations, movements of colonists, settlers, nomads and nomadic groups, migration stories, FX for novels, etc Zie ook: RGCG

Code.CodeDescription: Forced displacements, removals or population transfers
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: forced migration, forced relocation, forced population resettlement, involuntary migration, mass expulsions of peoples. Use with: N* codes for works about historical events and with relevant PLACE 1K* or 1QB* and TIME PERIOD 3* Qualifiers, Zie ook: NHTZ

Also class here: Contemporary slavery, forced labour, forced marriage, sexual slavery, modern-day slavery, forced prostitution, child labour, debt bondage, bonded labour, compelled labour, descent-based slavery, child slavery, child marriage, domestic servitude, or works about enslaved people or people who have been trafficked or are victims of modern slavery, human trafficking or sex trafficking Zie ook: NHTS

Code.CodeDescription: Geweld en misbruik in de maatschappij
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: ill-treatment, maltreatment or wilful neglect in society, violence based on cultural traditions, violence against particular groups or individuals, violent civil disorders, group or mob violence in society, vigilante justice, institutional violence, violent criminal behaviour in society etc. Use for: works about perceptions of violence and insecurity in society, as well as works on actual violence, abuse and neglect. Use with: JBSF* codes for gender-based violence Zie ook: JKV
Also class here: child neglect
Also class here: sexual violence, rape, sexual assault. Use with: JBSF1 for works about sexual violence against women and girls Zie ook: JKVN

Also class here: domestic violence, family violence, intimate partner violence, coercive control, gaslighting, master suppression techniques and countermeasures. Use with: JBSF1 for works about domestic violence against women and girls

Also class here: mobbing, social media trolling, cyberbullying, intimidation, coercion, stalking and threatening behaviour. Use with: JBCT* codes when linked to different kinds of media, KNXC or KJMV2 for workplace harassment

Code.CodeDescription: Controle, privacy en veiligheid in de maatschappij
Code.CodeNotes: Use for: issues and debates around privacy, use of data, the role of government and big corporations, security, anti-terrorism, rights of the individual versus the rights of society, surveillance, public safety, social control and coercion Zie ook: JPV

Also class here: Ableism, disablism, social aspects of neurodiversity, accessibility, inclusive practices. Use for: works that look at societal barriers to a person with impairments, the way societies treat disabled persons, the impact of policies, works about any form of discrimination, negative attitudes, assumptions or prejudice towards groups or individuals based on ability or disability, and works that look at ways to address these discriminations, address stereotypes, assumptions, social justice, etc. Use with: 5PM* Qualifiers as appropriate and other codes for specific topics, such as JBFA for discrimination, JBFD for housing topics, JKS* for welfare, NHTB for social history, FX for novels etc

Code.CodeDescription: Gezondheid, ziekte en verslaving: sociale aspecten
Code.CodeNotes: Use for: studies of the social or cultural impact of health policies or different illnesses or addictions; social or cultural behaviour or reactions to different types of addictions, illnesses, diseases or health scares, works that look at the social aspects of access or lack of access to health services, healthcare, health education, topics linked to the social aspects of planning access to health care, problems linked to lack of access or restrictions to healthcare services, etc. Use with: MBP to indicate social aspects of health systems

This style has inspired many comics around the world and use of this code does not mean the comic is published or created in the USA, only that the work is seen as being an example of that style of comic book

Code.CodeDescription: Amerikaanse stijl stripboeken: klassiek, Golden Age

Also class here: OEL manga, Original English-language manga (and similar concepts in other languages), Manga-influenced comics, World manga, Global manga, La nouvelle manga, Manfra, Amerimanga, etc. Use for: XAM* codes includes all Japanese style comic books (Manga) plus those from other East Asian countries including Korean style (Manhwa) and Chinese style (Manhua) and from non-Asian countries, but designed according the ‘Manga or East Asian styles’. Use with: XQ* codes to give detail of subject or genre and other subject A*– W* OR Y* categories and qualifiers where appropriate
Use with: XQ* codes to give detail of subject or genre and other subject A*– W* OR Y* categories and qualifiers where appropriate

Code.CodeDescription: Classic East Asian style / tradition comic books
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: classic East Asian style comics (Manga, Manhwa, Manhua, etc) which can usually be read and enjoyed by everyone from children to adults, and which are widely regarded or presented as ‘classic’ and typically but not necessarily published and in print for several decades
Use for: Manga or other East Asian style comics for children, boys and girls, of an interest age from around 6 to 10. Use with: 5A* qualifiers to indicate interest age
Use with: XQ* codes to give detail of subject or genre and other subject A*– W* OR Y* categories and qualifiers where appropriate
Use with: XQ* codes to give detail of subject or genre and other subject A*– W* OR Y* categories and qualifiers where appropriate
Use for: Manga or other East Asian comics designed for primarily younger teenage girls, adolescent females, of an interest age from around 10 to 15. Use with: 5A* qualifiers to indicate interest age

Use for: Manga or other East Asian style comics designed primarily for younger teenage boys, adolescent males, of an interest age from around 10 to 15. Use with: 5A* qualifiers to indicate interest age
Use for: Manga or other East Asian style comics designed primarily for older teenage boys, young adult and adult men, from about 15 years old and up
Use for: Manga designed primarily for older teenage girls, young adult and adult women, from about 15 years old and up

Use for: Manga or other East Asian style comics designed for adults featuring scenes of an overtly adult nature only suitable for an aware and mature audience. Use with: other XAM* codes as appropriate and Qualifier 5X as appropriate Zie ook: XAMX2
Use for: Manga or other East Asian style comics designed for adults (over about 18 years), of an extreme erotic or pornographic nature. Use with: Qualifier 5X as appropriate Zie ook: XAML

Also class here: shoujo-ai, baihe. Use for: Manga or other East Asian style comics featuring young female same-sex relationships often (but not exclusively) for a young female readership. Use with: 5PSL as appropriate
Also class here: post-underground comics, independent comics, indie comics, auteur comics, small press comics, new wave comics, creator-owned comics, art comics, underground comix, etc

Code.CodeDescription: Graphic novel, stripboek, en manga: genres
Code.CodeNotes: Use all XQ* codes with: F* or YF* codes, as applicable, to give further extra level of details of fiction genres where required, or, for non-fiction, with A*–W* or relevant Y* codes, as applicable, to indicate the key subject of narrative, for example a comic about an action war story use with FJM*, but one where war or conflict is the background, use with FXF

Code.CodeDescription: Graphic novel / stripboek / manga: memoires, waargebeurde verhalen en non-fictie

Use for: titles published as comics or manga where the content is primarily non-fiction and aimed at educating people about the subject. Use with: YN* codes if for young people or other relevant non-fiction A*– W* codes for titles aimed at adults, and use with relevant XA* code to indicate type. If created for use in educational institutions use with YP* codes and EDUCATIONAL PURPOSE 4* Qualifiers as appropriate, for graphic medicine or other comics about health or medical or public health topics use with VF* codes or YPJJ6 for educational works for schools, or educational titles about science or technology, use with P* or T* codes or YPM* codes

Code.CodeDescription: Graphic novel / stripboek / manga: literaire adaptatie
Code.CodeNotes: Use for: adaptations of pre-existing literary works into graphic form. Use with: DB*, DC*, DD*, F*, YF*, YND* or YPC* codes as appropriate

Code.CodeDescription: Graphic novel / stripboek / manga: film en tv-adaptaties
Code.CodeNotes: Use for: stories that were published as spin-offs or companions to pre-existing non-book media or merchandise, for example story books based on a popular film franchise, an online game or a TV series. DO NOT USE: for titles that were subsequently made into films etc

Code.CodeDescription: Graphic novel / stripboek / manga /manga: misdaad, mysterie en thrillers
Code.CodeNotes: Use with: FF* or FH* YFC* codes to give further details of crime or thriller genres where required

Code.CodeDescription: Graphic novel / Stripboek / Manga: Maatschappij / cultuur
Code.CodeNotes: Also class here: chroniques sociales, contemporary cultural, political or social topics or issues, comics that present aspects of the arts, culture, food, cuisine, music or society either as a story or as a work of non-fiction, etc. Use with: codes from A*– W* for works of non-fiction aimed adults to give more specific details about the topic covered or Y* codes for works aimed at children or teenagers, to give further details where required
